name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,286

clue.text: Greek hero cool in receding waters

indicators.note: something receding draws back the way it came, so the letters run backwards
one thing sitting in another means it is placed within the other's letters

blocks.note: a sea is a body of water
to chill is to cool

explanation.surface: A hero of Greek myth keeps his composure as the tide goes out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' sounds like a description of the hero's temperament, but it is a verb meaning to make cold; 'waters' is the setting that wraps around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Achilles is the great warrior of the Trojan War in Homer's Iliad, so he is an example of a legendary figure from Greece.

indicators.note: to grab is to take hold of, so one set of letters clasps another

blocks.note: in Genesis Cain kills his brother Abel, the first murder
apt means fitting or suitable

explanation.surface: The Bible's first killer seizes a leader who is in good shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' suggests physical health, but here it is the adjective meaning suitable. The container goes in just after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A captain is the person in charge of a team, ship or unit, so the word is a synonym for someone who heads a group.

indicators.note: the letters wanted lie inside the run of text that follows, spanning a word break

blocks.note: the end of the first word joined to the start of the second

explanation.surface: Something is still sitting inside a shipping container at a port terminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like an adverb meaning 'yet', but it is the adjective meaning motionless; the answer runs across contaINER Terminal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inert has no power of movement or action, so it is motionless, the adjective sense of the clue's first word.

blocks.note: first meaning: insolent talk, impudence
second meaning: one of the fleshy edges of the mouth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheek' reads as the side of the face, next to the mouth, but here it means sauciness.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving someone lip is backchat or impudence, and the same word names either fleshy rim around the opening of the face.

indicators.note: roaming means wandering freely, so the letters wander out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone on safari spots a big cat wandering through an East African park.
explanation.walkthrough: Tigers are Asian and not found in Tanzania, a small hint that the animal is only there for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti is a famous national park and wildlife area in northern Tanzania, known for its great migration of animals.

blocks.note: first meaning: thoughtful and caring towards others
second meaning: a type or category

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as 'a considerate type of person', but the two words are separate meanings, one adjective and one noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for gentle, generous behaviour and a noun for a class or variety of things.

blocks.note: kip is British slang for a sleep or to sleep
ling is another name for common heather

explanation.surface: An author settles down for a nap with a woman called Heather.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital H makes Heather look like a woman's name; it is the moorland plant, also called ling.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudyard Kipling was a British author of The Jungle Book and Just So Stories, so he is an example of a literary figure.

indicators.note: what is received is taken in, so one set of letters is taken inside another

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for earl
nice means pleasant or lovely

explanation.surface: A nobleman is welcomed into the home of a charming family member.
explanation.walkthrough: E sits inside NICE, between its I and C.
explanation.definitionFit: A niece is the daughter of one's brother or sister, so she is a family member by blood or marriage.

clue.text: Son breaks mirror in church recess

indicators.note: to break into something is to force a way inside it, so one letter goes within the others

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
to ape is to mimic or mirror someone

explanation.surface: A boy smashes a looking glass inside an alcove of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mirror' looks like a noun for a glass that could be broken, but it is the verb meaning copy.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the rounded or vaulted alcove usually at the east end of a church, beyond the altar.

blocks.note: first meaning: Cockney rhyming slang, where the phrase rhymes with lies
second meaning: savoury pastries that people happily eat

explanation.walkthrough: Swallowing lies means believing them, but here the swallowing is literal eating. In Cockney rhyming slang a word is replaced by a phrase that rhymes with it; 'porkies' is common British slang for fibs.
explanation.definitionFit: A pork pie is a British cold pastry filled with pork, and in rhyming slang the plural stands for untruths or fibs.

blocks.note: a mast is a tall pole on a ship
O is the abbreviation for old
a don is a fellow of a university college

explanation.surface: A Polish man, an elderly chap, used to be something of an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes 'Pole' look like a Polish person; it is a long post.
explanation.definitionFit: The mastodon was a large elephant-like mammal that is now extinct, so it is an animal that existed in the past.

indicators.note: going around something encloses it, so these letters wrap the next ones

blocks.note: passed, as in passed away, means died
still can mean yet, as in 'still to come'

explanation.surface: Something was handed round the room and is nonetheless untainted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passed around' reads as one phrase meaning circulated, but 'Passed' is the euphemism for died and 'around' is the wrapping signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Distilled liquid has been purified by boiling and condensing, so the word describes something refined and free of impurities.

indicators.note: something used in a thing forms part of it, so the letters sit within the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A notion is applied when studying the ebb and flow of the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across tIDE Analysis.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea is a thought or notion formed in the mind, a direct synonym for a mental conception.

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, and crazy letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, with the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A god of the Nile region is heard howling like a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' fits the jackal-headed god as if it described him, but it is the British slang for crazy ('barking mad') that signals the rearrangement. Nubia is the ancient land along the Nile south of Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: Anubis is the ancient Egyptian god of the dead and embalming, shown with a jackal's head, so he is a god.

indicators.note: to devour is to swallow whole, so one set of letters takes in another

blocks.note: a bear is a meat-eating animal
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing sizes
US is short for American, as in United States

explanation.surface: A meat-eater from the countryside wolfs down a big American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' could be an adjective meaning rural, but it is the definition: a nation. The size letter sits inside the animal and the American follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Belarus is a landlocked nation in Eastern Europe, bordering Russia, Poland and Ukraine, so it is an example of a state.

clue.text: Down covers bad leg in young bird

indicators.note: something bad is damaged or out of shape, so these letters are rearranged
a cover goes all round what it protects, so one set of letters encloses another

blocks.note: to down food or drink is to eat or swallow it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fluffy feathers protect an injured limb on a chick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' looks like the soft first feathers of a chick, which suits the scene, but it is the verb for swallowing food or drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An eaglet is the offspring of an eagle, a chick of that large bird of prey not yet fully grown.

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so these letters are altered in order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A physician who cannot see still manages to look at a cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' reads as a physician, a subject for the sentence, but it is the verb meaning tamper with. Ely is a small cathedral city in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no eyes means being unable to see, so the adjective is a literal way of describing sightlessness.

blocks.note: first meaning: a rubber sphere, one example of something that bounces
second meaning: a formal social gathering for dancing

explanation.walkthrough: A bouncer suggests a doorman guarding a dance venue; here it is simply a thing that bounces. In cricket a bouncer is also a short-pitched delivery.
explanation.definitionFit: The round toy that springs off the floor shares its name with a grand evening event where people waltz.

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so these letters go round another

blocks.note: taken as written
a row, rhyming with cow, is a noisy racket, a din
British motorways are numbered M1, M4 and so on

explanation.surface: An argument breaks out about how a highway is run.
explanation.walkthrough: A motorway is a British highway, labelled with M. M goes inside DIN, after A.
explanation.definitionFit: Admin is the informal short form of administration, the running and organising of an office or business.

clue.text: Man’s situation is as heir ruined

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked and broken up, so these letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man's circumstances are that he is an heir who has lost everything.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital M on 'Man' is the clue: it is the Isle of Man, an island between Britain and Ireland, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea, so that stretch of water is where the island is located.

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for heroin, which is also called by this animal's name
second meaning: a pony is a small breed of the animal

explanation.walkthrough: The italics mark Smack the Pony, a British TV sketch comedy show. Smack and the answer are both drug-world slang for heroin.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroin has street names including smack and this word, and a pony is a small member of that equine species.

clue.text: One held up in bad weather?

definitions.text: One held up in bad weather?

blocks.clueFragment: One held up in bad weather?
blocks.note: surface reading: a traveller delayed by storms, stuck at an airport
setter's reading: something literally raised above the head when it rains

explanation.walkthrough: 'Held up' means delayed in the surface; the answer is an object carried aloft over your head.
explanation.definitionFit: This rain shield is lifted over the head on a handle to keep a person dry during a downpour.

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
RC is the standard abbreviation for Roman Catholic

explanation.surface: A Catholic priest gives a reply while in Bow, a district of East London.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital B makes Bow look like the London district; it is a curve.
explanation.definitionFit: A bow is a curved shape, like the curve of a bent stick, and an arc is a curved line, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Bank charge right to be reversed

indicators.note: reversed means turned the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: a fee is a charge for a service
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A customer feels a bank's service fee ought to be cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank charge' reads as one financial phrase, but 'Bank' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A reef is a ridge of rock, coral or sand near the water's surface, and bank is another term for such a raised shoal.

definitions.note: a phrase, 'on us', meaning our responsibility

blocks.note: first meaning: a duty or responsibility
second meaning, split in two

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as ON US: what we must carry is on us.
explanation.definitionFit: An onus is an obligation or responsibility that weighs on someone, as in the onus of proof.

indicators.note: to block is to stand in the way, so one piece sits in the middle of another

blocks.note: a decree is an official order or edict
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: A government is overthrown at the moment it tries to obstruct an official order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When' is a small word easily read as a link, but it supplies letters; it goes in before the final letter of the order.
explanation.definitionFit: To decrease something is to reduce or lower it, a synonym for making numbers or amounts fall.
